STACK Infrastructure was launched January 16, 2019, per a trade press article from datacenterdynamics.com fetched this session, by IPI Partners, described in that article as a joint venture between Iron Point and Iconiq Capital. The new company launched with eight data centers across six United States markets and about 100 MW of capacity, built from two predecessor portfolios, three facilities from Infomart Data Centers in Ashburn Virginia, Portland Oregon, and Silicon Valley California, which IPI Partners had acquired in March 2018 after Equinix bought Infomart own Dallas headquarters building earlier that year, and five facilities from T5 Data Centers, a company IPI Partners had separately backed since 2016, in Atlanta Georgia, Chicago Illinois, and the Dallas Fort Worth Texas area, with T5 Data Centers itself continuing to operate separately afterward with remaining sites in Los Angeles, Charlotte, Colorado Springs, New York, and Cork City Ireland. Brian Cox, previously chief executive of Infomart Data Centers, became STACK Infrastructure own chief executive. STACK Infrastructure own about page, fetched this session, describes the company as a partner designing, developing, and operating global digital infrastructure, and states a current footprint of 10 metro markets in the Americas, 5 in Asia Pacific, and 7 in EMEA, 22 markets in total, though each market can itself include multiple campuses, for example Silicon Valley alone contains 3 campuses and Milan alone contains 11. reading.body:
Stack Infrastructure's STACK SVY02 in Santa Clara County publishes floor area but not power consumption, making it impossible to assess its role in AI infrastructure without additional disclosure.

The facility occupies 560,440 square feet across a single building on a 9-acre site in what was formerly Memorex headquarters. That scale places it among the larger data centers in Silicon Valley by physical footprint. The operator's public specification page does not, however, disclose megawatts of IT capacity, power density, or cooling architecture. Floor area alone cannot be translated into compute density or workload type without knowing how intensively the space is provisioned.

This gap matters because power is the limiting constraint on AI scaling. A facility of this size could support anywhere from modest colocation to high-density accelerator deployment depending on electrical and cooling infrastructure. Without that information, the site cannot be ranked against other California facilities or assessed for its contribution to regional AI infrastructure capacity.

California hosts 103 mapped facilities in this data set, of which only five have published power figures totaling 170 MW. STACK SVY02 is counted in the facility inventory but cannot be included in any power-based analysis. Its location in Santa Clara County places it at the center of the densest AI infrastructure cluster in the country, but public data does not yet reveal what its actual computational role is.
